info.title: Internal API
info.description:
# About

This API is for superuser access and machine-to-machine requests.

It allows for operations on resources by specifying the resource without consideration of account membership privileges. The admin section of the Account's frontend uses this API for example. The backend processes of other apps, like Trustedform and LeadConduit, can also perform operations through this API without needing a current browser session, for example.

## Authentication

Supported methods of authentication:
- Browser session
- Bearer token in the authorization header. This is a machine-to-machine token found in 1Password.

## Pagination

When making requests to endpoints that support pagination, you can use the following optional parameters:

- `page`: The current page number (default: 1)
- `per_page`: Number of records per page (default: 10)
- `offset`: The offset to start from (default: 0)

Example request:
```
GET /api/internal/resource?page=3&per_page=20&offset=10
```

Pagination information is included in the response headers:

- `X-Total`: Total number of records
- `X-Total-Pages`: Total number of pages
- `X-Page`: Current page number
- `X-Per-Page`: Number of records per page
- `X-Next-Page`: Next page number (if available)
- `X-Prev-Page`: Previous page number (if available)
- `X-Offset`: Current offset

## Kafka

### Overview

Kafka is used to share data with other teams and systems. By aligning Kafka events with our OpenAPI documentation, we address past challenges with undocumented SQS messages and inconsistent data structures between APIs and SQS messages. This approach ensures consistency and reliability, as the data structures are documented and standardized across both Kafka and our API. Our goal is to gradually publish as much data as possible, starting with `create`, `update`, and `delete` (CUD) events for each resource. Every topic will include CUD events, with the flexibility to add supplementary event types as needed. Additionally, for each resource, we provide two API endpoints to fetch either a single record or multiple records with pagination, ensuring multiple and flexible methods for retrieving data.

### Topic Naming Convention

Kafka topics follow a structured naming convention:

```
accounts.<resource>
```

Examples:
- `accounts.accounts`
- `accounts.domains`
- `accounts.network.invitations`

### Header Properties

Each Kafka event includes the following headers:

- **event-type**: Specifies the type of event (e.g., `created`, `updated`, `deleted`, etc).
- **event-version**: Represents the version of the OpenAPI schema that corresponds to the event's data structure.

Refer to the OpenAPI documentation for detailed data structures and schemas associated with each event.

tags.name: Companies
tags.description:
This resource serves as a directory of companies that have chosen to appear on the network. A company
profile describes a business who participates in the consent-based marketing industry.

To connect with a company, create a new connection invitation. Once recipient accepts your invitation,
a new connection will appear in the connections resource.

tags.name: Connections
tags.description:
A connection is made when one company on the network invites another to connect and
the receiving company accepts the invitation.

The owner of an offer can share it with other accounts on the network to which the owner is connected.
That gives the other account permission to participate in the offer. If it's a buyer-owned offer, the
buyer shares an offer with their sellers. And those sellers share it with theirs, and so on. If it's a
seller-owned offer, the seller shares it with their buyers. When the owner of an offer shares it with
another company on the network, an “Offer Share” is created.

tags.name: Connection Invitations
tags.description:
Invitations are the primary means two companies becoming connected. A company in the network invites
another company to connect. Invitations are emailed to the recipient of the invitation. The recipient
can accept or simply take no action.

If the recipient of the invitation does not belong to an existing company within the network, the
recipient will be prompted to create a new account.

If the recipient is already a member of the network and has memberships with multiple companies, the
recipient will be prompted to select the company with which they would like to connect.

Invitations expire after 30 days. If an invitation expires or the recipient did not receive the original
invitation, the sender can optionally resend the invitation. Resending an invitation will mark the current
invitation as pending and re-send the invite.

tags.name: accounts.network.invitations
tags.description:
## Connection Invitations

The `accounts.network.invitations` topic is responsible for tracking connection invitations between companies in our system. This topic publishes events when an invitation is created, updated, accepted, declined, or deleted.

## Headers

- **event-type:** Indicates the type of event. Possible values are:
  - `created`: Sent when a connection invitation is sent/created.
  - `updated`: Sent when any property on an invitation changes.
  - `accepted`: Sent when an invitation is accepted (also triggers `updated`).
  - `declined`: Sent when an invitation is declined (also triggers `updated`).
  - `deleted`: Sent when an invitation is deleted. Typically occurs if the associated company/account is deleted.

tags.name: Errors
tags.description:
The Errors resource provides standardized error responses for the API. All error responses conform to the [RFC 9457 - Problem Details for HTTP APIs](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457.html) specification in order to return consistent and detailed errors.

### Common Errors
- **400 Bad Request**: The request could not be understood or was missing required parameters.
- **401 Unauthorized**: Authentication failed or the user does not have permission for the requested operation.
- **403 Forbidden**: Authentication succeeded but the authenticated user does not have access to the requested resource.
- **404 Not Found**: The requested resource could not be found.
- **422 Unprocessable Content**: Validation errors occurred when processing the request.
- **500 Internal Server Error**: An unexpected error occurred on the server.

### Example Error Response
```json
{
  "type": "about:blank",
  "status": 422,
  "title": "Unprocessable Content",
  "detail": "The request could not be processed due to validation errors.",
  "errors": [
    { "pointer": "#/name", "detail": "can't be blank" },
    { "pointer": "#/email", "detail": "is invalid" }
  ]
}
```

status.description: The HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence of the problem.

type.description:
A URI reference that identifies the problem type. This URI provides context and additional
information about the specific kind of error that occurred, allowing clients to understand
the nature of the problem beyond the status code alone.

title.description:
A short, human-readable summary of the problem type. The `title` is intended to give a brief
overview of the issue, making it easier for developers and users to quickly understand the nature
of the problem without needing to delve into technical details.

detail.example: The request could not be understood by the server due to malformed syntax.
detail.description:
A human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence of the problem. The `detail` field
provides specific information about what went wrong in this particular instance, helping clients
understand the exact issue and how they might resolve it.

errors.description:
An array of objects containing information about errors in the request. Each object in the array
typically includes details such as the field that caused the error and a human-readable message
explaining the issue. This is particularly useful for validation errors where multiple issues
might need to be communicated to the client.

BadRequest.description:
**Bad Request (400)**

This entity represents a Bad Request error (HTTP 400 status code).
A Bad Request occurs when the API request parameters provided by the client
do not conform to the expected format or the OpenAPI schema defined for the endpoint.

Common reasons for a Bad Request include:
- Missing required parameters.
- Invalid data types.
- Parameters that fail validation checks according to the API's specification.

Clients should review their request against the API documentation to correct any issues
before resubmitting the request.
BadRequest.title: Bad Request

detail.example: The provided email address is invalid.
detail.description:
This field provides a detailed description of the error encountered, helping the client
understand what went wrong. It is particularly useful for validation errors or other
client-related issues. The `detail` should be clear and concise, providing enough
information for the client to identify and correct the problem.

pointer.description:
A JSON Pointer [RFC 6901] that indicates the location in the request entity
where the error occurred.

The `pointer` field provides a path to the element in the JSON document that caused the error.
This path is expressed as a JSON Pointer, as defined in RFC 6901, and it helps clients identify
the exact location of the issue in their request. The pointer typically follows the format of
`#/path/to/field`, indicating the hierarchical path within the JSON structure.

**Example:**
A pointer to the 'email' field in the request:
```json
"#/user/email"
```

Unauthorized.description:
**Unauthorized (401)**

This entity represents an Unauthorized error (HTTP 401 status code).
An Unauthorized error occurs when the client attempts to access a resource without
proper authentication or authorization.

This error typically happens when:
- The client fails to provide valid credentials.
- The credentials provided do not grant the necessary permissions to access the resource.

Clients should ensure they are authenticated and have the appropriate permissions
before retrying the request.

InternalServerError.description:
**Internal Server Error (500)**

This entity represents an Internal Server Error (HTTP 500 status code).
An Internal Server Error occurs when the server encounters an unexpected condition
that prevents it from fulfilling the request.

Common causes of an Internal Server Error include:
- Unhandled exceptions or runtime errors within the server.
- Issues with server configuration or dependencies.
- Resource limitations, such as memory or disk space constraints.

This error indicates a problem on the server side that the client cannot resolve.
Clients may need to retry the request later or contact support if the issue persists.
